Most of my clients live in a different time zone than I do.
Jakarta, Berlin, New York, Sydney. For a long time my “system” was a world clock, a to-do app, a spreadsheet for hours and a separate tool for invoices. I kept asking myself the same question every day: what time is it for my client right now, and when should I send this?
So I built the tool I wanted. Meet Taskly  😊 
Under the hood: React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind and Supabase, deployed on Cloudflare. It works offline first, syncs in real time across devices, and every table is protected with Row Level Security.
What I learned: the hardest part of remote freelancing isn’t the work itself. It’s the coordination around it. Good tools should quietly remove that friction.
If you work with clients across time zones, I’d love your feedback. What is the one thing that slows you down the most?

Every order used to be a long WhatsApp thread. 💬

Price lists, stock checks, shipping quotes per city, matching bank-transfer screenshots… all by hand. For a small florist, that means missed orders and lost custom requests.
So I built Pinkara Studio a real online flower shop. 🌸

From browsing to delivery, everything now runs in one place:
→ Mobile-first storefront with variants & add-ons
→ Live JNE / J&T shipping rates across Indonesia
→ QRIS & virtual account payments with a live countdown
→ Order tracking, cancellations & refunds
→ Custom bouquets: brief → chat → quote → pay in one click
→ An admin dashboard so the owner never misses an order

But the part I'm most proud of is what you don't see.

E-commerce gets messy when things happen at the same time:
• Double-click "Place order"? Still just one order.
• 8 buyers grabbing the last item? Only 1 wins, and stock never goes negative.
• "First 5 buyers" promo? Exactly 5, even under load.
• Payment arrives at the last second? No clash with the expiry job.

Money and stock have to stay correct, always.

Many investors focus on acquiring land in Indonesia. Fewer focus on whether they could lose it.

Indonesia's new Agrarian Reform Law (Law No. 10 of 2026) may become one of the most important legal developments for businesses with significant landholdings, yet I suspect many investors have not fully considered its implications.

Most commentary has focused on the Law's policy objectives: reducing inequality, resolving agrarian conflicts and supporting agrarian reform. Those objectives are important. However, from an investor's perspective, the more immediate question is:

Could this law affect existing landholdings, future acquisitions, development projects or investment exits?

The answer may be yes.

Why should investors care? The Law introduces:

⚠️ A powerful new agency with authority to resolve agrarian disputes and issue binding decisions.

⚠️Priority agrarian reform areas, potentially affecting land within designated locations.

⚠️ Potential group-wide limits on landholdings, not just limits at the individual company level.

⚠️ New requirements for some HGU holders, particularly those operating large land banks.

For me, the most significant issue is not the text of the Law itself.

It is the fact that many Indonesian transactions already involve some degree of land risk, whether arising from overlapping claims, community occupation, historical use, licensing issues or competing rights. Investors often become focused on valuation, financing and transaction execution, while assuming land matters can be resolved later.

That assumption may become more difficult to make.

If I were advising a private equity fund, infrastructure investor, energy developer, plantation company, industrial estate operator, data center developer or multinational seeking to expand in Indonesia, I would be asking three questions:

1. Which assets could become exposed to agrarian reform measures or conflict claims?

2. Does our current land due diligence adequately identify those risks?

3. How might these issues affect future refinancing, acquisition or exit processes?

The implementing regulations will be critical and are likely to receive close attention from investors over the coming months.

Every week you wait, your shortlist shrinks.

Here is the part of hiring nobody puts in the report: your best candidates are not waiting for you. While your panel finds a date, aligns on criteria, and debates the ranking, those candidates are taking other interviews and accepting other offers.

By week three, the shortlist you finally approve is often not the shortlist you started with. It is whoever is left.

The delay rarely comes from a lack of candidates. It comes from screening without a decision system: CVs read one by one, notes in different formats, 'good feel' debated in a meeting with no agreed bar for what good means. Every handoff adds days, and every day costs you a candidate you already liked.

The fix is not rushing the decision. It is deciding faster on purpose: agree the shortlist criteria before you post, screen in structured batches instead of one-off reads, and rank every candidate against the same bar so the panel debates evidence, not impressions.

Teams that do this do not just hire faster they hire from the full shortlist, not the leftovers.
